text: Order-notifications, the service scaffolded in Lesson 29, is ready for its first real release past dev. Acme-corp's platform team wants every promotion to staging and prod to ship as a canary -- a small slice of traffic first, watched automatically, promoted or rolled back without a human babysitting a dashboard. This lab wires that up end to end, on top of the same GitOps repo structure Chapter 4 already established.

The first move is swapping the plain Deployment for a Rollout, Argo Rollouts' own kind that understands progressive traffic shifting natively. The container spec and resource limits stay identical to before -- only the strategy block is new. Traffic moves in four scheduled steps, ten percent, twenty-five, fifty, then a hundred, pausing five minutes between each one.

A pause by itself only waits -- it doesn't look at anything. The real decision comes from an AnalysisTemplate that queries Prometheus for the canary's error rate on every pause. The success condition requires that rate to stay under one percent, and crossing it twice fails the analysis outright, with no human needing to notice first.

Promoting a new version still looks exactly like ordinary GitOps: commit a new image tag, push, and ArgoCD syncs the change the normal way, because the Rollout and its AnalysisTemplate are just more YAML in the same overlay Chapter 4 already wired up. From there, the AnalysisRun watches automatically at every pause step, with no dashboard-watching required.

If the canary's error rate crosses that threshold twice, Argo Rollouts aborts entirely on its own -- traffic returns to the stable revision, the canary pods scale to zero, and the Application in ArgoCD shows the failed promotion as out of sync. The whole failure and recovery stays visible in Git and in ArgoCD exactly as it happened, with no manual rollback command and no incident call needed to stop a bad release from reaching everyone.

Lesson 30 proved a real canary rollout with automated rollback, still entirely inside GitOps. Lesson 31 steps back from the mechanics to ask a harder question: what happens when a platform team builds all of this correctly, and developers still don't use it.
